Battery Testing (Real World):

In this section, I just want to quickly outline the battery burn over a few different activities, as well as daily life.

For daily battery burn, I was mostly using the 47mm Fenix 9 Pro inReach model, with it usually set for ‘Auto’ as the LTE/Satellite configuration. This meant that it would essentially leverage my phone as needed for LTE connection, and then save battery otherwise. In this configuration, I was getting around 5ish days of battery life, but that’s inclusive of roughly 1-2 hrs of GPS workout time per day (some days more, some days less, but on average). This is in the ballpark of what I saw on a similar 47mm Fenix 8 Pro unit. I believe this is slightly short of the official Garmin claim in terms of smartwatch battery life, but that claim assumes 30 minutes of GPS time per day, rather than my reality of 4x that.

Next then, the more interesting ones, is GPS battery burn across various units/activities. In this case, I tried to make these as identical as possible. That included setting up identical settings/configurations/etc…

First, this gravel ride. Solar on one side, AMOLED on the other, both 47mm units. No LTE enabled on this one, nor any navigation. Just riding, power meter connected, and LiveTrack via the phone. This is using the default satellite configuration mode.

As you can see, the solar unit has nearly 3x the battery life in this scenario closer to sunset. On this ride, there were very few trees to block the sun, and equally, on the outbound direction, the unit was facing the sun.

Next, a road ride, mid-day. Here we can see substantially less battery life for the Solar unit, though, about the same ~40hr estimate for the AMOLED. This again shows how variable the solar benefit can be. Again, this is using the default satellite configuration mode. My wife wore her 43mm unit as well, though you can see in that configuration with her profile, it was burning far more battery than the next test with my settings.

Next, we’ve got a 10hr hike. This started before sunrise, and then finished later in the day. Placement was one per wrist, and one per hand. In theory, that might mean the hand-units (the 51mm and 43mm) might have needed to work slightly harder for optical HR, though I had them strapped in pretty tight, so I doubt it.

(The orange strap one is the 47mm AMOLED, the blueish/grey strap one on the upper hand is the 51mm AMOLED, then down below the smaller black strap is the 43mm AMOLED, and the lower left one is the 47mm SOLAR)

Given it was a one-way hike, the Solar unit was facing the sun almost the entire time, which would have significantly helped it. Equally though, there were trees and rocks and cliffs and such that blocked it. This is pretty real-world, assuming real world is a Mediterranean island with what is still summer sun. All units had an identical course loaded, and for the most part I was on general data fields, except when I needed to double-check the map briefly, or climbing with ClimbPro. All units were using optical HR.

Next, we’ve got about 6.5hrs out on the water, with a Solar vs AMOLED test. This was an out-and-back route, so roughly speaking it should be a wash in terms of solar time. You can see here that again, pretty consistently, the AMOLED floats at about 40hrs of battery life (estimate). The Solar was double that. There were no trees/mountains, or even clouds out here, though I did take occasional dips in the water.

Finally, here’s another fun 6.5hr activity out on the water, this time with the LTE configuration forced on the entire time. This meant that it was constantly trying to update my LiveTrack location via LTE (since I had LiveTrack enabled, and my phone connection disabled). Further complicating matters, is that a fair chunk of this area had no cellular location, thus, it probably was trying even harder at times. Anyways, here’s the result of that:

As you can see, forcing it into LTE definitely took a chunk out of the battery life there. I suspect the first/last portion being ‘flat’ was because I was mostly stopped then versus moving, and definitely 100% in LTE coverage then. It’s unclear to me which factor was more important.

As always, I could rabbit-hole for weeks/months on different battery tests/configurations. But in short, I think this gives you a rough idea of what to expect for different amounts. As always, solar will usually be more than AMOLED, though equally, all of these tests were done in super sunny weather where I live – with virtually no cloud cover. If you live/etc in a place with overcast skies, you’re simply not going to get anywhere near this much extra solar battery life. You will still benefit though from the battery gains of a MIP screen, though how much is kinda variable on a lot of factors.

Equally, one can remember that you could reduce the accuracy level slightly and get far more battery life out of the Fenix 9 AMOLED units too. Or, you could add a chest strap to gain battery life, etc… Meaning, there’s lots of other tradeoffs you could make if you don’t want MIPS/SOLAR, but want more battery life than shown here.

Software Stability & Bugs:

This section is dedicated to the issues and bugs I saw during my Fenix 9 series testing, including both bugs I saw as well as my wife saw. This includes all units/models I have in my possession. After the extremely rough buginess/stability of the recent Garmin Cirqa release, which has followed more than 18 months of generally less stable releases from Garmin, I was keen to see how things would handle on the Fenix 9.

Overall, this is an improvement over the Cirqa release, though, not without its bugs. Most of these bugs were not ‘mission critical’ (meaning, they didn’t block me from completing a workout, and didn’t cause full loss of an entire workout). Instead, they were just annoying. All of these are present on the current/final/production firmware. These are things like empty/incorrect data pages, unexplainable messages, high battery burn on one watch, and more. Examples include:

– Stress score missing on-device, saying it needs three consecutive days of data, despite being worn 24×7 for weeks
– Endurance Score sporadically missing on-device, saying it needs two weeks of data, and then showing up again half a day later. Rinse/repeat
– Numerous bugs/errors around Garmin Epic’s, and especially around not properly enumerating activity data from multiple workout types over a time span. It’s clear there wasn’t enough testing on this scenario (e.g. doing swim/bike/run activities as part of an Epic, but also having a course for some of it)
– Rucking activity not initially sending LiveTrack or course data during workouts (this appears to have been a one-time thing)
– Unable to sync/update maps via Mac on Garmin Express (even on MacOS26)
– Super high battery burn rates on my wife’s 43mm unit (two different units). However, when I reset the unit and put my profile on it, the battery burn seems normal. Meaning, this may be tied to some bug/issue on some setting within her profile, rather than mine or the watch.

Next, there’s the not-exactly-bug category that as of this past week, Apple released MacOS27, and with it has broken Garmin Express for Fenix 9 users. Oddly, this did actually work on MacOS27 during the summer.  The singular area that matters for 99% of users, if you have to download a new map region (e.g. going to North America from Europe). While you can do that over WiFi, it takes approximately forever/hours. The map update with the Fenix 9 specifically and Garmin Express are different than the Rosetta issue, however. As a side note, Garmin has recently splintered the map regions a bit into slightly smaller chunks, which makes the WiFi slightly more viable from a hotspot in a hotel room as I found out last week. Either way, Garmin says they’re going to update Garmin Express sometime before the end of the year, but that doesn’t really help people today – no matter the Mac-related issue they have.

Finally, I have had multiple crashes – both on my watch and my wife’s watch. In my case, it was during a trail run where it just randomly reset/crashed as I was running down a hill, for no obvious reason/interaction. I was able to resume the run/activity a few mins later, though lost the time in between when it crashed and when it resumed. In the case of my wife’s, it crashed while she was drinking a glass of wine. Twice, I think. In her case, the only thing she lost was her focus on the wine consumption. Fear not, though, given there’s no Wine Readiness Score, she wasn’t dependent on her Garmin watch to complete her adventure.

Wrap-Up & Final Thoughts:

The Fenix 9 feels in many ways like what the Fenix 8 Pro launch should have been: A cohesive story of all the models getting updates with satellite connectivity, new sport features, and plenty more. Which isn’t to say the Fenix 8 Pro launch was bad, but rather, it wasn’t a complete picture. The Fenix 9 solves that. And for the most part, it does so quite well and quite reliably. Setting aside the bugs I had above, all my activities have recorded without issue, navigation without issue, and other Fenix 9 Pro inReach features without issue. I genuinely appreciate that when my wife goes out for her late night long runs alone (without a phone), I’ve got tracking on her. Even if it’s just to drop-off some more snacks. Something that wasn’t possible in the Fenix 8 Pro series, because it didn’t have a small enough unit for a small female wrist.

If we look at the new features of the Fenix 9 series, I appreciate the sport focus here. The addition of a slate of rowing features, Ski Erg features, and other sports things is great. I’ve haphazardly done indoor rowing when the moment fits, but this actually has me a bit more excited to do more indoor rowing (and have been scouring Facebook Marketplace for a used unit). Perhaps that’s silly, or perhaps that’s no different than any other bit of motivation people have from smartwatches today (be it hitting step goals, closing rings, streaks, or the such). And for those actual rowers, this finally makes a Garmin device capable of truly tracking their training loads.

One of the most notable things about the Fenix 9 release isn’t the Fenix 9 itself. It’s Garmin’s decision, the first in some 15+ years, to actually bring software updates to a previous-generation watch (the Fenix 8 and Fenix 8 Pro are considered the same ‘generation’ from a Garmin standpoint, despite being a year apart). This is a massive shift in Garmin’s stance, and one I suspect is being driven by how their competitors approach software updates (including Apple, COROS, and others). However, just as notable is this is only the 2nd time in Garmin’s 14-year history of the Garmin Fenix series, the non-Pro and Pro models were announced at the same time (the other being in 2019). Historically speaking, those would flip-flop every year. That flip-flop led to ever-more-confused consumers thinking that the ‘Pro’ model was a higher-end model, when in reality it was simply the next year’s model. This shift remedies that, yet also maintains the new annual Fenix release cycle appended to UTMB, for the second year in a row (previously it floated at every 14-18 months).

Overall, I think this is a fairly solid launch for Garmin. They’ve maintained the ‘choice’ aspect of the Fenix lineup (e.g. display types, sizes, etc…), done so without increasing the prices over previous crazy-pants prices, and delivered on most of the features that people wanted coming out of the Fenix 8/Fenix 8 Pro series. All while concurrently delivering those software features back to the Fenix 8 owners. Hopefully this is the ‘new Garmin’ that we get to keep for a while.

With that, thanks for reading!
